steps.prompt: How does a sentence become a finished song?
steps.sub: You type "upbeat lofi for studying" and out comes a real, polished track. That's not one button — it's a small assembly line. By the end of this you'll know every stage, what each one does, and why the order matters.

steps.prompt: First instinct — what does an AI music pipeline actually do?

options.t: Plays back songs that already exist, like a streaming app.
Takes your prompt or lyrics, generates audio, then mixes and masters it into a finished track.
Records you singing and auto-tunes your voice.

steps.why: A music pipeline starts from your intent (a prompt and/or lyrics), generates raw audio, then cleans it up through mixing and mastering — ending in a finished, shippable track. It isn't a player (no new audio is made) and it isn't a vocal recorder (you don't sing into it).
hints: Two of these only handle audio that already exists. Which one creates new audio AND finishes it?
Think 'factory line', not 'play button'. What comes IN, what comes OUT?

steps.sub: Tap each card. These four turn an idea into a track you can publish.

cards.b: Your intent in words: style, genre, mood, BPM — plus optional lyrics to be sung.
The model turns that intent into raw audio — vocals and/or instruments.
Balance the parts: levels, EQ, panning — so nothing is muddy or buried.
Final loudness + polish so it sounds pro and consistent on every device.

steps.prompt: Tap the 4 stages in the order they run.
steps.sub: Each stage feeds the next — get the order wrong and you're polishing nothing.
chips: Mix the parts into a balanced track
hints: You can't generate audio before you've told it what you want.
Mastering is the LAST polish — it only makes sense after the parts are already mixed.

steps.sub: Tap an item, then tap the stage it belongs to.

items.t: Model produces a 2-minute raw audio file
Turn the bass down so it stops drowning the vocal

hints: Anything you write in WORDS before any audio exists is the prompt/lyrics stage.
'Balance the parts' = mix. 'Final loudness for every device' = master.

steps.prompt: Why split 'mix' and 'master' into two stages instead of one?
steps.sub: They sound similar but do different jobs.

options.t: There's no real difference — it's just two names for the same step.
Mixing balances the parts WITHIN the track; mastering polishes the FINISHED track as a whole for loudness and consistency across devices.
Mixing is for vocals and mastering is only for instruments.

steps.why: Mixing works inside the song — getting drums, bass and vocals to sit together. Mastering treats the already-mixed song as one finished object and makes it loud, even, and consistent whether it plays on earbuds, a phone speaker, or a car. Different scope, different goal — that's why they're separate.
hints: One stage looks at the PARTS inside the song. The other looks at the WHOLE finished song.
Which step is about 'sounds pro on every device'?

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: The same engine and pipeline can make a song, a lofi beat, or focus music — only the prompt changes.
statements.why: Yes — the stages stay the same; you steer the output by changing what you ask for. One factory, many products.

statements.t: If you skip mastering, your track will play just as loud as commercial songs.
statements.why: No — without mastering your track is usually quieter and less consistent, so it feels weak next to mastered Spotify tracks. Mastering is the loudness/polish step.

statements.t: The output of the pipeline is a finished audio file (like an MP3 or WAV) ready to publish.
statements.why: Right — that finished, mastered file is the whole point. Everything before it exists to produce it.

hints: Think about why 'one engine, many genres' is a selling point.
Mastering is the loudness step — what happens to volume if you skip it?
